propositions.text: The principal claimant and family members from Colombia and the USA claim refugee protection in Canada under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, his partner XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, their daughter XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of Colombia, and their sons XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of the United States of America, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant and family from Colombia and the USA claim refugee protection in Canada under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: The principal claimant accepted being the designated representative for his minor children as per IRPA subsection 167(2) and RPD Rule 15.
propositions.quote: As per subsection 167(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and Rule 15 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, the principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, confirmed at the hearing that he accepted being the designed representative for his minor children.

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant accepted being the designated representative for his minor children as per IRPA subsection 167(2) and RPD Rule 15.

propositions.text: The panel is satisfied as to the claimants' identities based on copies of their passports submitted on file.
propositions.quote: Given the copies of the claimants' passports submitted on file,1 the panel is satisfied as to their identities.

paragraphs.summary: The panel is satisfied as to the claimants' identities based on copies of their passports submitted on file.

propositions.text: The principal claimant alleged certain facts relevant to the refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant alleged the following facts.

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant alleged certain facts relevant to the refugee claim.

propositions.text: From 1986 to 1989, the claimant worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.
propositions.quote: From XXXXX 1986 to XXXXX 1989, he worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX of XXXXX, Colombia.

paragraphs.summary: From 1986 to 1989, the claimant worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.

propositions.text: The claimant resigned due to threats received mostly at his mother's residence from members of popular militias (FARC, EPL, ELN) who never identified themselves.
propositions.quote: He resigned from his position as a XXXXX XXXXX because of threats (telephone calls) received mostly at his mother's residence. According to the claimant, the authors of the threats were members of various popular militias (FARC, EPL and ELN). However, also according to the claimant, the authors of the threats never identified themselves.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant resigned due to threats mostly at his mother's residence from popular militias who never identified themselves, according to him.

propositions.text: After resignation, claimant moved multiple times for safety and continued receiving calls trying to recruit him to militias instead of just threats.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that, after this resignation, he moved a number of times for his own safety and that during this time, he continued to receive telephone calls at his mother's home. However, the callers then tried to recruit the claimant for various popular militias instead of just uttering threats of reprisals because of his work as a XXXXX XXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: After resignation, claimant moved multiple times for safety and continued receiving calls trying to recruit him to militias instead of just threats.

propositions.text: From 1996 to 1997, claimant worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.
propositions.quote: From 1996 to 1997, he worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX of XXXXX, Columbia.

paragraphs.summary: From 1996 to 1997, claimant worked as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.

propositions.text: Claimant resigned in 1997 due to telephone threat at work from militias and for safety of family.
propositions.quote: He resigned as a XXXXX XXXXX in 1997 because some members of various popular militias had found him. The claimant stated that he received a telephone threat at work during this time. The claimant stated that he resigned from that position for his own safety and that of his family.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant resigned in 1997 due to telephone threat at work from militias and for safety of family.

propositions.text: From 1997 to 1999, claimant worked as a security XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.
propositions.quote: From 1997 to 1999, he worked as a security XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, XXXXX Sector, XXXXX, Colombia.

paragraphs.summary: From 1997 to 1999, claimant worked as a security XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in Colombia.

propositions.text: Claimant resigned in 1999 due to threats from different popular militias.
propositions.quote: He resigned as a XXXXX XXXXX in 1999 because of threats from different popular militias.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant resigned in 1999 due to threats from different popular militias.

propositions.text: Claimant did not file police complaints because judicial institutions in Colombia are infiltrated by militias, increasing danger.
propositions.quote: He did not file any complaint with the police or any other authorities in Colombia regarding these threats because the judicial institutions in Colombia have been infiltrated by the popular militias and filing a complaint would only have increased the dangers that he already faced.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant did not file police complaints because judicial institutions in Colombia are infiltrated by militias, increasing danger.

propositions.text: Claimant left Colombia for the USA in 2000 to join wife and daughter.
propositions.quote: He left Colombia for the United States of America in 2000 to join his wife XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and his daughter XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant left Colombia for the USA in 2000 to join wife and daughter.

propositions.text: Claimant returned to Colombia in 2002 to see if he could live safely and to obtain documents for US asylum claim.
propositions.quote: He returned to Colombia in XXXXX 2002 to see whether he could live there without being threatened and to obtain documents to facilitate a claim for asylum in the United States of America.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant returned to Colombia in 2002 to see if he could live safely and to obtain documents for US asylum claim.

propositions.text: Claimant returned to USA in 2003 to file asylum claim but decided chances better in Canada after lawyer advice.
propositions.quote: He returned to the United States of America in XXXXX 2003 in the hopes of filing a claim for asylum for himself and the members of his family. He then determined, after receiving advice from a number of lawyers, that his chances of success were better in Canada than in the United States of America.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant returned to USA in 2003 to file asylum claim but decided chances better in Canada after lawyer advice.

propositions.text: Claimant claimed refugee protection for himself and family in Canada on XXXXX, 2008 at Lacolle, Quebec.
propositions.quote: He claimed refugee protection for himself and his family on XXXXX, 2008, at Lacolle, Quebec, Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant claimed refugee protection for himself and family in Canada on XXXXX, 2008 at Lacolle, Quebec.

propositions.text: The minor sons are US citizens and did not submit evidence about fear regarding the USA.
propositions.quote: The claimants, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, the minor sons of the claimants, are citizens of the United States of America. The claimants did not submit any evidence pertaining to their fear regarding the United States of America.

paragraphs.summary: The minor sons are US citizens and did not submit evidence about fear regarding the USA.

propositions.text: The panel determines claimants did not demonstrate reasonable fear of persecution if returned to Colombia.
propositions.quote: After examining all of the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimants did not discharge their burden of demonstrating a "reasonable fear of persecution" should they return to Colombia.

propositions.text: The panel also determines claimants have not shown on balance of probabilities that they are persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel also determines that the claimants have not demonstrated that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be "persons in need of protection".

paragraphs.summary: The panel determines claimants did not demonstrate reasonable fear of persecution or need of protection if returned to Colombia.

propositions.text: Whether an internal flight alternative is determinative in these refugee claims.
propositions.quote: The panel believes that an internal flight alternative is the determinative question in these claims for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Claimant fears militias still present and will try to recruit him again if returned to Colombia.
propositions.quote: In reply to the question [translation] "What would you fear should you return to your country?" the principal claimant replied that he fears that the people who were trying to recruit him into the popular militias are still there and will try to recruit him again.

propositions.text: Panel repeatedly asked if specific identifiable people might present danger but claimants could not answer; threats were anonymous calls.
propositions.quote: The panel repeatedly asked whether specific and identifiable people might possibly present a danger to the claimants, but the claimants were not able to answer. According to the claimants, the threats were made anonymously over the telephone.

paragraphs.summary: The panel sees internal flight alternative as key; claimant fears militias still present but threats were anonymous and no specific danger identified.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Colombian militias recruit voluntarily, forced recruitment prohibited, candidates usually illiterate aged 15-30; claimant is almost 45.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence2 on file demonstrates that in Colombia, recruitment by popular militias, more specifically the FARC, is conducted on a voluntary basis and that forced recruitment is prohibited. Candidates sought are usually illiterate and between the ages of 15 and 30. In this case, the claimant is almost 45 years old.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges telephone calls continued trying to recruit him even after leaving Colombia over 10 years ago; mother still receives calls.
propositions.quote: According to the claimant's testimony, the alleged authors of the telephone calls never stopped trying to recruit him, even though he left Colombia over 10 years ago. Also according to the claimant, his mother is still receiving telephone calls at her home inquiring as to the claimant's status and his interest in joining the popular militias.

propositions.text: Panel finds it highly unlikely militias still try to recruit claimant 10 years after departure and claimant failed to show these attempts could lead to reprisals.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that it is highly unlikely that the militias are still trying to recruit the claimant 10 years after his departure from Colombia. Furthermore, the claimant was not able to satisfy the panel that these attempts to recruit him could turn into reprisals if he did not acquiesce to this pressure to recruit him, since he was not subject to any direct threat and he did not submit any evidence to that effect.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant's allegation of ongoing recruitment attempts is implausible and undermines his credibility.
propositions.quote: The panel concludes that the claimant's allegation that the alleged authors of the telephone calls continued to try to recruit him after he left Colombia and are still doing so today is implausible and therefore undermines the claimant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Evidence shows militia recruitment is voluntary and claimant's ongoing recruitment claims are implausible, undermining his credibility, panel finds.

propositions.text: The principal claimant was questioned about fears if returned to other parts of Colombia, like Bogota.
propositions.quote: the principal claimant was questioned about what he might fear should he return to live elsewhere in Columbia-in Bogota, for example.

propositions.text: The panel gave claimants opportunity to present evidence but gave no reason why returning to Colombia would be unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the panel ensured that the claimants were given the opportunity to present their evidence, they did not provide any reason as to why it would be unreasonable, as outlined by the jurisprudence,3 to return to their country to find refuge.

propositions.text: No real and concrete evidence was submitted showing risk of persecution or cruel treatment if returned to Colombia.
propositions.quote: Nor did they submit any real and concrete evidence establishing that current conditions are such that they would face persecution under one of the Convention grounds or a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant was questioned about fears of returning to Colombia, but the panel gave no reason why return would be unreasonable and found no concrete evidence of risk.

propositions.text: The panel believes claimants could move to another city in Colombia.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that the claimants could move to another city in Colombia.

propositions.text: The principal claimant stated he was not threatened but solicited by militias after resigning from police.
propositions.quote: At his hearing, the principal claimant stated that he had not actually been threatened, but had been solicited by members of the popular militias after he resigned from the police force.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the panel believes claimants could relocate in Colombia; claimant said he was solicited but not threatened by militias.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimants failed to prove on balance of probabilities that relocating to Bogota would cause fear for their lives.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that the claimants were not able to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that relocating within Colombia, more specifically to Bogota, would cause them to fear for their lives.

propositions.text: Claimants argue militia authors of calls could find them anywhere in Colombia.
propositions.quote: The claimants' main argument is that the alleged authors of the telephone calls could find them anywhere in Colombia.

propositions.text: The panel finds it highly unlikely militias would pursue the principal claimant elsewhere in Colombia.
propositions.quote: The panel is of the opinion that it is highly unlikely that the popular militias would feel the need to find and pursue the principal claimant elsewhere in Colombia.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants failed to prove fear if relocating to Bogota; claimants argue militias could find them, but panel finds pursuit unlikely.

propositions.text: The panel concludes it is not unreasonable or too harsh to expect claimants to move to Bogota before claiming refugee protection abroad.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the panel concludes that it is not objectively unreasonable to believe, or too harsh to expect, that the claimants could move to Bogota before claiming refugee protection abroad.

propositions.text: Claimants failed to prove militia authors of calls would pursue or try to find them.
propositions.quote: The claimants were not able to prove that the alleged authors of the telephone calls would have any interest in pursuing or trying to find them.

propositions.text: According to principal claimant, call authors were trying to recruit him to their organization.
propositions.quote: To the contrary, according to the principal claimant, the authors of the calls were attempting to recruit him to their organization.

propositions.text: It is highly unlikely the principal claimant is of such interest to militia authors that they would try to find him in Bogota.
propositions.quote: It is highly unlikely that the principal claimant could be of such interest to the alleged authors of the telephone calls that they would try to find him in Colombia, more specifically Bogota.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes it is reasonable to expect claimants to move to Bogota; they failed to prove militias would pursue them there, as calls were recruitment attempts.

propositions.text: Burden of proof for internal flight alternative rests on claimant to show unreasonableness or conditions preventing relocation.
propositions.quote: ...the burden of proof regarding an internal flight alternative rests on the claimant...Thus, the applicant had to establish either that it would be unreasonable for her to seek refuge in another part of the country or that there were, in fact, conditions preventing her from relocating elsewhere...

propositions.text: Jurisprudence confirms burden is on claimant to show unreasonableness of seeking refuge elsewhere in country.
propositions.quote: It is settled law that in matters concerning internal flight alternatives the burden of proof is on the applicant... Therefore, the refugee claimant must demonstrate that it would be unreasonable for him or her to seek refuge in a different part of the country.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held claimant must show serious risk of persecution in part of country providing internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal established that the onus is on the claimant to demonstrate why, on a balance of probabilities, they face a serious risk of persecution in a part of the country that could provide an internal flight alternative.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites jurisprudence that the claimant bears the burden to prove internal flight alternative is unreasonable or unsafe.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimants did not discharge burden of proof and have an internal flight alternative in Bogota.
propositions.quote: the panel is of the opinion that the claimants did not discharge their burden of proof as established by the jurisprudence7 and concludes that they have an internal flight alternative in Bogota, Colombia.

propositions.text: Finding of internal flight alternative suffices to dispose of refugee claim under IRPA sections 96 or 97(1).
propositions.quote: this finding by the panel is sufficient in itself to dispose of the claim for refugee protection, regardless of whether the claim refers to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants failed burden and have internal flight alternative; this suffices to reject refugee claim under IRPA.

propositions.text: The panel determines claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: the panel determines that the principal claimant and the members of his family are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.

propositions.text: The panel rejects the claimants' refugee protection claims.
propositions.quote: their claims for refugee protection are rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the claimants' refugee protection claims.
